articleSummary: Ebola virus disease is an acute viral illness caused by Ebola virus, with an average fatality around 50%. Six species are known: Zaire (most lethal, up to 90%), Sudan (40–60%), Bundibugyo (25–40%), Tai Forest (rare), Reston (infects primates and pigs and does not cause disease in humans), Bombali (bats; no human cases). First identified in 1976 near the Ebola River in South Sudan and the DRC; outbreaks occur mainly in sub-Saharan Africa. Transmission occurs via wildlife-to-human contact with infected blood, secretions, or organs (fruit bats are the natural reservoir); human-to-human spread through direct contact with bodily fluids and contaminated environments, including during funerals; healthcare workers and sexual transmission (rare) are risk factors. Incubation 2–21 days; early symptoms include fever, weakness, muscle pains, headache, sore throat; later vomiting, diarrhea, rash, kidney/liver dysfunction, bleeding. Treatment is supportive—hydration and symptom care, ICU for severe cases. FDA-approved monoclonal antibodies (Inmazeb, Ebanga) target Zaire Ebola; Ervebo vaccine (Zaire) is used for outbreak control but is not registered in Hong Kong. Preventive measures: strict hand hygiene, avoid contact with sick individuals and wild animals, and ensure thoroughly cooked foods.

articleSummary: Ebola, Bundibugyo ebolavirus, has reawakened global concern with the World Health Organization declaring an outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo (Ituri province) and Uganda (Kampala), and issuing a public health emergency of international concern, though not a pandemic. By the weekend, Ituri reported 80 suspected deaths, eight laboratory-confirmed cases, and over 336 suspected cases; the DRC health ministry confirmed 80 deaths. In Kampala, two laboratory-confirmed cases were recorded, including one death, linked to travelers from DRC. A laboratory-confirmed case was also reported in Kinshasa (Ituri returnee). The outbreak began in a busy mining district, with the index patient—a nurse in Bunia—on April 24. Bundibugyo-type Ebola lacks approved therapies or vaccines. The WHO warns numbers may be higher due to testing, and regional spread risk is elevated; recommends activated national emergency systems, enhanced border/transport surveillance, without closing borders. Africa CDC and US CDC assist with surveillance, lab testing, and contact tracing.

articleSummary: An Ebola outbreak in the Ituri province of the Democratic Republic of the Congo linked to Bundibugyo virus has 246 suspected cases, 8 confirmed, and 80 deaths (CFR 32.5%) as of May 16, 2026. The WHO declared this outbreak a Public Health Emergency of International Concern (PHEIC) on May 17, 2026, signaling global vigilance though not a pandemic. Travel-associated cases have been reported in Kampala, Uganda, and Kinshasa. Transmission occurs through direct contact with blood, body fluids, or contaminated objects from infected humans or animals, entering via skin or mucous membranes. Symptoms include fever, malaise, myalgia, headache, vomiting, diarrhea, and possible bleeding; incubation is 2–21 days. There is no widely available specific treatment; management is primarily supportive, and vaccines are limited. The Ministry of Health, DR Congo, Uganda, and WHO have mobilized rapid response teams, surveillance, supplies, and risk communication, emphasizing cross-border vigilance and expedited referral.

articleSummary: Bundibugyo ebolavirus, a relatively rare Ebola strain, has triggered a WHO public health emergency of international concern. The outbreak is spreading in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) and Uganda, with the strain first identified during a 2007–2008 outbreak in Bundibugyo District, Uganda. There is no approved vaccine or specific therapy for Bundibugyo. Fatality has historically ranged from 30% to 50%, lower than some Zaire ebolavirus outbreaks that can reach 70–90%. Transmission occurs through direct contact with blood or body fluids, contaminated objects, or contact with infected animals; it is not airborne. Symptoms include fever, malaise, muscle aches, headache, vomiting, diarrhea, and bleeding in severe cases. Factors raising concern include delayed detection, conflict and mining areas, limited health facilities, and cross-border movement between Uganda and DRC. Key controls: early detection, isolation, PPE use, and robust contact tracing.

articleSummary: WHO declares Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) and Uganda a Public Health Emergency of International Concern (PHEIC) due to rising cases, cross-border spread, and uncertainties about scale, linked to Bundibugyo strain. As of May 16, DRC's Ituri Province reported eight laboratory-confirmed cases, 246 suspected cases, and 80 suspected deaths; cases have reached Kinshasa and Uganda, where two infected individuals traveled from DRC and were admitted to intensive care. The outbreak is likely larger than detected, with clusters of unexplained deaths, high test positivity, and limited understanding of transmission. At least four healthcare workers have died. No approved vaccines or specific treatments exist for Bundibugyo; research and trials are urgent. WHO advises strengthened surveillance, contact tracing, testing, infection control, and treatment capacity, plus community engagement; avoids travel/trade restrictions. An Emergency Committee will reconvene.

articleSummary: Outbreak of Bundibugyo Ebola virus in northeastern Democratic Republic of Congo (Ituri and North Kivu) with about 350 suspected cases and 91 deaths; Uganda reports two infections (one death in Kampala) and a separate case in Goma, eastern Congo. WHO declared a public health emergency of international concern on Sunday due to cross-border spread, healthcare-worker infections, and uncertainty about the true scale after a four-week detection delay. Bundibugyo has had only two prior outbreaks and has no approved vaccine or antibody treatment. Early symptoms, fever, weakness, headache, vomiting, diarrhea, mimic malaria. Initial tests for Zaire were negative; Bundibugyo confirmation came May 14. Rapid tests may not reliably detect Bundibugyo, highlighting the need for Bundibugyo-specific diagnostics in central/east Africa. Many suspected cases in Ituri and North Kivu remain under investigation in a conflict-affected region.

articleSummary: Ebola Virus Disease (EVD) is caused by several Ebolaviruses—primarily Ebola, Sudan, and Bundibugyo—with an average fatality around 50%, differing by outbreak. First identified in 1976 in South Sudan and the Democratic Republic of Congo. Fruit bats are the probable natural reservoir; transmission to humans occurs via contact with infected wildlife and, in humans, through blood or bodily fluids, contaminated surfaces or instruments, with burial rites fueling spread. Incubation is 2–21 days; early symptoms are nonspecific, progressing to severe disease with internal and external bleeding, liver and kidney failure, and neurological disturbances. Diagnosis requires PCR, antibody, and antigen tests, plus viral isolation in specialized labs; samples must be handled with extreme care. Treatment is mainly supportive (fluids, symptom relief, management of co-infections), with some antibody-based therapies approved; vaccines exist, notably ERVEBO, to limit outbreaks. Prevention relies on public health measures to reduce exposure.

Major human outbreaks involve three species: EBOV (Ebola virus disease), SUDV (Sudan virus disease), and BDBV (Bundibugyo virus disease). Transmission begins with animal-to-human spillover, typically via fruit bats, and spreads between people through contact with blood or body fluids and contaminated objects, placing health workers at risk. Incubation is 2–21 days; early symptoms include fever, fatigue, and sore throat; severe cases involve vomiting, diarrhea, kidney/liver impairment, and bleeding. Case fatality averages about 50% (range 25–90%). No cure exists; care is supportive. Monoclonal antibodies mAb114 and REGN-EB3 improve survival; control relies on care, infection prevention, surveillance, contact tracing, safe burials, vaccination where applicable, and community engagement.

articleSummary: As of 2026-05-18, Congo faces its 17th Ebola outbreak since 1976, driven by the Bundibugyo strain, for which no licensed vaccine exists. Bundibugyo causes rapid fever, vomiting, diarrhea and bleeding, with a 30–50% case fatality rate. The index case appears to be a nurse who died at Bunia’s Evangelical Medical Centre, with exposure chains extending weeks before official detection. A patient who traveled to Uganda and died in Kampala, then had the body transported back to DRC for burial, highlights cross-border transmission risks. Diagnostic tests in the field often miss Bundibugyo; unlike the Zaire strain, there are no validated rapid tests or approved vaccines. Ring vaccination with rVSV-ZEBOV (Ervebo) helped quell Zaire outbreaks, but cannot address Bundibugyo. Ituri province’s isolation and conflict, plus limited PPE manufacturing, impede response.

More than 2,600 laboratory-confirmed human cases have been reported to WHO, with about 84% in Saudi Arabia. Sporadic cases and small clusters have occurred outside the region, including the United Kingdom, usually in travelers from the Middle East. articleSummary: Japan supplied the antiviral Avigan (favipiravir) from national stockpiles to Britain on Friday in response to a hantavirus outbreak linked to a cruise ship voyage in the Atlantic Ocean. Britain accepted the drug under a bilateral memorandum of understanding; aboard the ship, a Japanese national was among those monitored after the voyage. There is no established cure for hantavirus, but animal studies suggest Avigan may improve survival; the shipment does not reduce Japan's stockpiles. Health Minister Kenichiro Ueno thanked Britain for accommodating the Japanese national on a chartered plane and for ongoing health observations, reaffirming Tokyo's commitment to international cooperation to prevent spread. Separately, Ueno noted the WHO's Public Health Emergency of International Concern over Ebola outbreaks in Congo and Uganda and urged calm, saying domestic risk remains low.
notes: 記事はハンタウイルスの大西洋船舶集団発生と、別のイベントとしてWHO PHEIC指定されたコンゴ・ウガンダのエボラ流行に言及。対象国リストに基づき、DRCのみverified_locationsに含める。ウガンダはリストに含まれないため除外。日本・英国は主題の流行発生地ではなく、対応国として登場するため除外。

articleHeadline: WHO declares Ebola outbreak in Congo, Uganda an emergency of international concern
articleSummary: Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo and Uganda declared a public health emergency of international concern (PHEIC) by the WHO, caused by Bundibugyo virus. The outbreak involves 80 suspected deaths, 8 lab-confirmed cases, and 246 suspected cases in DRC’s Ituri province (Bunia, Rwampara, Mongbwalu) with one confirmed case in Goma. In Uganda, two lab-confirmed cases have been reported in Kampala, including one death, linked to travel from the DRC. About six Americans in the DRC have been exposed; one may have developed symptoms. The CDC activated its emergency response center and plans to deploy more staff. No Bundibugyo-specific therapeutics or vaccines exist. The outbreak poses international spread risk but does not meet pandemic criteria; measures call for isolation, daily contact monitoring, restricted travel after exposure for 21 days, and cross-border screening, while discouraging broad border closures.
notes: 発生地域にUganda（226074）とRwanda（49518）が含まれているが、記事サマリーではDRCでの主要な発生とウガンダでの限定的な確認例（2例、1死亡）が述べられている。対象国リストに含まれるのはDRCのみであるため、verified_locationsはDRCのみとした。WHOによるPHEIC宣言は感染症危機管理の観点から極めて重要なシグナル。CDC緊急対応センター啓動も確認。Bundibugyo型エボラウイルスは特異的な治療法やワクチンが存在しないことも懸念要因。

articleHeadlineTranslated: Ebola epidemic in Africa: WHO sounds the second-highest alert — how high is the risk to Europe?
articleHeadline: Ebola-Epidemie in Afrika: WHO schlägt zweithöchsten Alarm - wie groß ist das Risiko für Europa?
articleSummary: As of 18 May 2026, the World Health Organization declared the Ebola outbreak in Ituri Province, Democratic Republic of the Congo, and Uganda a Public Health Emergency of International Concern (PHEIC), the second-highest alert level after a pandemic. The Bundibugyo ebolavirus strain drives this outbreak; there are no vaccines or therapies for this variant. The Ituri region borders South Sudan and Uganda and is a busy mining area with large displaced populations amid conflict. The overall risk to Europe remains theoretical but not zero; earlier European cases involved returning healthcare workers, while the general population outside Africa bears very low risk. Transmission occurs through direct contact with blood, secretions, bodily fluids, or contaminated materials, not via the air. Containment hinges on rapid case identification, isolation, contact tracing, and protecting health workers. Case fatality is about 25–40%, depending on diagnostic speed and care quality.
notes: ウガンダも発生地域として記載されているが、サマリーでの記述はIturi Province（DRC）が主体。ウガンダの具体的な患者発生の明記はないため、検証済み位置はDRCのみ。PHEIC宣言は最高レベルの国際関心事項。ワクチン・治療法なし、致死率25-40%と極めて高リスク。

articleHeadlineTranslated: Indonesia reports three hantavirus cases.
articleHeadline: Индонезия выявила три случая хантавируса
articleSummary: Indonesia reports three hantavirus cases. An outbreak of hantavirus occurred on the Dutch cruise ship MV Hondius, which was sailing from Argentina to Cape Verde. Three people died. The vessel arrived at the Canary Islands on May 10, and passengers were evacuated. On May 12, the World Health Organization reported 11 hantavirus infections linked to the voyage, with 9 laboratory-confirmed as Andes virus infections. The incident underscores international travel-related risk and the need for surveillance of imported cases. No nationalities of the affected individuals are provided. The voyage originated in South America, with Canary Islands serving as the evacuation point for passengers headed toward Europe/Africa. As of May 12, the outbreak comprises 11 infections, 9 Andes virus confirmations, and 3 deaths.
notes: 記事サマリーの主題は国際航海中のハンタウイルス集団感染で、インドネシアがアルゼンチナからカーボベルデへの航海中に3例を報告。カナリア諸島（スペイン領）での乗客避難、WHO報告の11例確認(Andes virus 9例確認、死亡3例)。発生地域にはアルゼンチナ、スペイン、カーボベルデも記載されているが、記事サマリーの主題はインドネシアの報告であるため、対象国リスト内で検証できるのはインドネシア(1643084)のみ。国際的な渡航関連リスク顕著。

articleHeadlineTranslated: Ebola outbreak erupts in neighboring Congo; Uganda postpones annual religious activities.
articleHeadline: 邻国刚果暴发伊波拉疫情 乌干达推迟年度宗教活动
articleSummary: On May 17, 2026, Ebola was confirmed in Goma, an eastern city of the Democratic Republic of Congo, where hospital staff screen visitors with thermometer guns before entry. The DRC's northeast has reported about 350 suspected Ebola cases and 91 deaths. Uganda has confirmed two infections and one death. In response, Ugandan President Yoweri Museveni announced on May 18 that the June 3 Martyrs’ Day religious festival will be postponed to protect public health, with a new date to be announced later. Martyrs’ Day commemorates 45 Ugandan men killed for their faith between 1885 and 1887; 22 were declared Blessed in 1920 and canonized as saints in 1964.
notes: Bluedot APIの発生地域にはUganda（Republic of Uganda）が含まれているが、記事サマリーではウガンダは「隣国で確認」という受動的な立場であり、主たる疫情発生地はDRCである。ただしウガンダで感染確認（2症例、死亡1）と既に国際的拡大が見られる。エボラ出血熱という最高リスク疾患であり、350疑い症例・91死亡報告、政府レベルの対応（宗教活動延期）、複数国関与により、シグナルとして最優先でピックアップ。
